hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever had something stolen, or lost something you really cared about?
options: it does. this story has a thief in it too.

steps.line: Freed at last, Epictetus taught philosophy in Rome. Then the emperor Domitian threw the philosophers out of the city.
So he crossed to Nicopolis, on the western coast of Greece, and opened a school. Young men came from far away to sit on his benches.
At home he kept a small shrine with an iron lamp beside it. One night he heard a noise at the door, and ran down.

steps.q: The lamp is gone. What do you think Epictetus says?
o: “I need a lock on the door”
steps.why: He doesn’t chase anyone. He buys something nobody would bother to steal.

steps.line: The lamp was gone. He thought: the thief did nothing strange. Thieves steal.
“Tomorrow,” he told himself, “you will find an earthen lamp. For a man only loses that which he has.” A clay one.

steps.q: Epictetus wasn’t a birth name. It’s a Greek word. What does it mean?
steps.why: Epiktetos means “acquired.” He was born enslaved, owned by a man in Nero’s court, and taught that what’s truly yours can’t be taken.

steps.line: Later he told his students: I lost a lamp. The thief paid more. For a lamp, he became a thief.

steps.q: Why does Epictetus say the thief paid more than he did?
o: He risked prison for a cheap lamp
He traded his honesty for a lamp
He’d have to sell it for less
steps.why: Epictetus lost an object. The thief lost a piece of himself.

steps.line: Today: the bike gone, the cut lock still on the rack. Epictetus would say: not “I lost it,” but “I gave it back.”
steps.label: today

steps.q: “Not ‘I lost it,’ but ‘I gave it back.’” Gave it back to whom, for Epictetus?
o: To the giver, who’d only lent it
To the thief, who wanted it more
To nobody, it’s just a saying
steps.why: In his Handbook: never say “I lost it,” say “I gave it back.” Care for things the way travelers care for an inn, not as owners.

say: here’s what i love. an emperor took his city. a thief took his lamp. he kept teaching anyway, and he kept his sense of humor.
his word for the part that can’t be taken was prohairesis: your will, your choice of how to meet what happens. the school at nicopolis had benches and walls. the real school was inside him.

steps.q: After he died, someone paid a fortune for his clay lamp, hoping some of his wisdom came with it. What would Epictetus probably say?
o: “Keep it lit, and think of me”
steps.why: Lucian says a man paid three thousand drachmas for it, hoping to grow wise by its light. The wisdom was in how Epictetus met losing it.

today.say: his handbook has a practice for this: never say “i lost it.” say “i gave it back.” today, if something small slips away, a parking spot, a pen, an hour, say it his way, and notice what’s still yours: your temper, your kindness, your next choice.
options: good. that’s prohairesis, in real life.
it’ll come in handy sooner than you think.

card.keepWhy: You only lose what you have.
sources: Epictetus, Discourses 1.18.15–16 (George Long, 1890): “I also lately had an iron lamp placed by the side of my household gods; hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp; for a man only loses that which he has.”
Epictetus, Discourses 1.29.21: he lost a lamp because the thief was more wakeful; the thief paid for it by becoming a thief.
Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 15.11.5: when Domitian expelled the philosophers, Epictetus left Rome for Nicopolis.
Arrian, preface to the Discourses (he wrote down his teacher’s words); prohairesis as will or choice.
Lucian, The Ignorant Book-Collector 13: a man bought Epictetus’s earthenware lamp for three thousand drachmas, hoping its light would bring him Epictetus’s wisdom.
Epictetus, Enchiridion 11 (Long): “Never say about anything, I have lost it; but say I have restored it.”

check: When Epictetus was freed is unknown (“freed at last”); the date of Domitian’s expulsion (about 89 or 93–95 AD) is debated.
The household shrine (“household gods”) is shown as a small niche with figurines. Confirm.
Hard one: Lucian says the buyer hoped that reading by the lamp at night would bring him Epictetus’s wisdom in his dreams; “after he died” is implied, not stated. Confirm.
